title: Linear and logistic regression: regularisation and reading the coefficients

videos.script: Every kilometre adds two and a half minutes. Rain adds eleven. A rush hour adds ten. {{weights}} That is a delivery model, and you can read the whole of it out loud. {{read}} It is a line. It cuts the error of lesson two's best rule nearly in half, with five columns and no tuning. {{line}} This lesson fits two of them. A line for a number, the minutes. And a line bent into a probability, for the churn question. {{logistic}} Along the way, three traps. A weight is not a cause. Weights in different units cannot be compared. And with too few rows, a line finds patterns in pure noise. {{traps}} The cure for the last one has a name, regularisation. You will watch it push forty noise columns to zero. {{lasso}} The logistic model makes less money than lesson two's box. So why fit it at all? Because it is the strongest baseline there is, and it tells you whether the data makes sense. {{end}}
